A well-known review of brainstorming studies found that people who worked alone and then pooled their ideas beat the same number brainstorming face to face, for both quantity and quality, and the gap grew as groups got bigger.[^A] More recently, a study of idea generation at Wharton tested a hybrid: people think alone first, then meet to share and choose. Where: After "The Perfect Brainstorm", as a boxed exercise
Proposed text:
TRY IT: BRAINWRITING

Brainstorming goes wrong when people wait their turn, copy each other and slow down. Brainwriting fixes that by making everyone write first.

1. Write the problem as a question at the top of a sheet of paper (Chapter 4 shows how). Sit in a group of four to six.
2. Everyone silently writes three ideas on their own sheet in five minutes. No talking.
3. Pass your sheet to the person on your left. Read what is there, then add three more: build on one of the ideas, or go somewhere new.
4. Keep passing until every sheet has been all the way round, or the ideas dry up.
5. Only now talk. Stick the sheets up, group the ideas that belong together and vote for the strongest few.

Why it works: nobody waits for a turn, the quietest person gets as many ideas down as the loudest, and every idea can spark another. In one study, groups who passed written ideas around this way outperformed people working alone.[^D]

Time: 30 to 40 minutes. Group: four to six. Materials: paper and pens.
Why: Gives readers a group technique that fixes the problems the chapter describes (blocking, copying, downward norm setting), instead of leaving them with 'brainstorms are a mixed blessing'.
Evidence / source: D: Paulus and Yang (2000), Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 82(1), 76-87. Abstract: groups sharing ideas in a brainwriting paradigm outperformed non-sharing (nominal) groups during the session and in a later individual session. The slips-of-paper procedure comes from a secondary summary; I did not read the paper. The five steps are the authors' adaptation of the standard method, not the study's protocol.
Confidence: Medium (the study result is verified at abstract level; the exact procedure is not)
Notes: Adds about a third of a page in the designed PDF. I left out the "6-3-5" name and its German origin because I have not verified the source; say if you want it.

Proposed text:
SPAGHETTI ON TAP

Until recently, the hard part of idea spaghetti was making enough of it. AI has changed that. In a 2023 study, researchers at Wharton and Cornell set GPT-4 against Wharton students on a simple task: ideas for a new product for college students that would cost less than $50. The chatbot produced around 200 ideas in about 15 minutes, many times what a person manages in that time, and when the ideas were rated by how likely people said they would be to buy the product, 35 of the best 40 came from the chatbot.[^E] That is a lot of spaghetti.

There are two catches. First, the ideas tend to be alike. A 2025 study found that ideas brainstormed with ChatGPT were more similar to one another than ideas from people working without it.[^F] (Chapter 1 reports the same pattern in stories.) Second, no machine can tell you which of 200 ideas is worth your next year. When ideas are cheap, the scarce skills are the knife and fork: choosing, combining and caring enough to see an idea through. We come back to choosing in Chapter 11.
Why: The 2010 chapter is about making more ideas. In 2027 a reader will ask what AI does to that, and the chapter's own metaphor (a plate of spaghetti without a knife and fork) answers it. This follows the freshness-map plan for Chapter 2.
Evidence / source: E: Girotra, Meincke, Terwiesch and Ulrich (2023), 'Ideas Are Dimes a Dozen: Large Language Models for Idea Generation in Innovation', SSRN working paper. 200 ChatGPT-4 ideas in about 15 minutes; top-10 percent by purchase intent: 35 AI, 5 student (this figure comes from a Wharton Executive Education summary, not the paper). F: Meincke, Nave and Terwiesch (2025), 'ChatGPT decreases idea diversity in brainstorming', Nature Human Behaviour 9(6), 1107-1109. I verified the title and citation; I did not read the paper. The 'Chapter 1' cross-reference is to the Doshi and Hauser result already in Chapter 1 (C1-37).
Confidence: Medium. The GPT-4 study is a working paper and the 35-of-40 figure is second-hand. The ChatGPT diversity finding is verified at title level only.
Notes: Needs Mark and Dave to approve the last sentences (the authors' view). Models change quickly; I would add a note saying GPT-4 is now several generations old, as in Chapter 1. If the "top 40" figure cannot be checked against the paper, delete that clause and keep "around 200 ideas in about 15 minutes".
